introduction: “It is incumbent upon all men, each according to his ability, to refute the arguments of those that have attacked the Faith of God.” Bahá’u’lláh set the terms at once: by “pen and tongue,” never by violence. The first third of these hundred quotations shows what that meant in practice: accusations investigated and exposed; replies that are “moderate, tempered, and infinitely courteous”; books by Mírzá Abu’l-Faḍl studied so that others can answer; forged and altered histories annotated in the margin. The middle of the guide belongs to years of danger, when gatherings were kept small, travellers needed a signed letter, and those spreading doubts were to be avoided; the images are of a fortress, of watchmen, of wolves among sheep. It ends with the fearlessness of the Manifestation Himself. The New Testament letters come from a community in the same position and say the same things, often in the same images: give an answer with meekness, let good conduct silence slander, beware of wolves, test the spirits. Nehemiah built with a weapon in one hand. Against the readings’ caution stand Mill and Jefferson on the free hearing of error, Jesus’s silence before Pilate, his rebuke of the disciples who wanted fire from heaven, and the two proverbs about answering a fool.
questions: “Moderate, tempered, and infinitely courteous.” Recall an attack on something you hold dear. What would a reply in that spirit have sounded like?
“Whatsoever ye commit, the people attribute to the Source of the Cause.” In what sense is conduct the first defence of a faith?
Proverbs says both “answer not a fool” and “answer a fool.” What guidance do the readings give for telling the cases apart?

Travellers without a letter were not to be received, and those raising doubts were to be avoided. Mill and Jefferson would let error speak freely. What conditions made the readings’ caution necessary, and do those conditions hold where you live?
The fiercest readings speak of flame, lightning and a sword, all of the tongue. How do the first readings limit what such images can mean?
“There is an answer in the teachings for everything,” yet many lack the scholarship to give it. What would you need to study to answer the objection you hear most often?

outside.why: All are to refute attacks on the Faith, each according to ability, by pen and tongue. Peter: be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear.

“Rather than have recourse to sword or violence.” Locke draws the same line: every man has commission to admonish, exhort, convince another of error; but to compel with the sword belongs to none but the magistrate.
Jude: ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
The accusation was investigated and the accuser exposed. Proverbs: he that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him.
The Qur’án: if an evil-liver bring you tidings, verify it, lest ye smite some folk in ignorance.
A reply should be “moderate, tempered, and infinitely courteous.” The Qur’án: reason with them in the better way.
“Look not at the language used by that hostile writer.” Jude: Michael the archangel, when contending with the devil, durst not bring against him a railing accusation.
Proverbs: a soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger.
Anyone with doubts is invited to state them and be answered. Mill: he who knows only his own side of the case, knows little of that.
“We do not attack, neither calumniate … we bring forth proofs and arguments.” Paul’s manner: three sabbath days he reasoned with them out of the scriptures, opening and alleging.
They answer with whatever they can think of against us. Paul: being reviled, we bless; being defamed, we intreat.

Whatever believers do, “the people attribute to the Source of the Cause.” Paul to Titus: shew thyself a pattern of good works, that he that is of the contrary part may be ashamed, having no evil thing to say of you.
Peter on the defence that conduct makes: so is the will of God, that with well doing ye may put to silence the ignorance of foolish men.
The learned must be defenders of the faith, by learning. Paul’s requirement of an elder: that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.
“Be vigilant in all regions regarding the Cause of God.” Ezekiel: if the watchman see the sword come, and blow not the trumpet, his blood will I require at the watchman’s hand.
Those who protected the friends in times of danger “will not be forgotten.” Hebrews: remember them that are in bonds, as bound with them; and them which suffer adversity.
Some opponents are not to be confronted. Nehemiah to those who kept inviting him to a meeting: I am doing a great work, so that I cannot come down.

Proverbs gives both counsels in consecutive verses: answer not a fool according to his folly, lest thou also be like unto him. Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he be wise in his own conceit. How do the readings decide when to answer and when to stay silent?
A tampered history must be shown for what it is. Nicodemus, to a council that had already decided: doth our law judge any man, before it hear him, and know what he doeth?
Record each alteration in the margins and explain it. Deuteronomy’s rule for a serious charge: enquire, and make search, and ask diligently.
The Bábí leaders “composed treatises” in reply. Apollos: he mightily convinced the Jews, and that publicly, shewing by the scriptures.
History, the writer says, is his object, not argument. Milton trusted the open contest: let Truth and Falshood grapple; who ever knew Truth put to the wors, in a free and open encounter?
In Baghdad scholars and princes came with questions and were answered. Jesus’s promise: I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which all your adversaries shall not be able to gainsay nor resist.
“Though not wearing the garb of the people of learning,” He reasoned with great scholars. The council on Peter and John: they perceived that they were unlearned and ignorant men, and they marvelled.
Proofs presented to the divines. Paul before a king: the king knoweth of these things, before whom also I speak freely; for this thing was not done in a corner.

Bahá’ís prove Christ to the Jews and Muhammad to the Christians. Justin Martyr, the first Christian apologist, was as generous to the Greeks: those who lived reasonably are Christians, even though they have been thought atheists; as Socrates and Heraclitus.

Missionaries’ books against Muhammad were answered. The Qur’án’s own rule for speaking of another’s faith: revile not those unto whom they pray beside Allah, lest they wrongfully revile Allah through ignorance.

“They had heard many things which were not true.” Tertullian on what was believed of the early church: if the Tiber rises, if the Nile does not, if there is famine or pestilence, straightway the cry is, The Christians to the lion!
The most useful books demonstrate the Cause “with logical proofs.” Luke’s reason for writing: that thou mightest know the certainty of those things, wherein thou hast been instructed.
“There are times that one is obliged to speak.” Peter and John: we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard.

Jesus before Pilate chose otherwise: he answered him to never a word; insomuch that the governor marvelled greatly. What does silence say that an answer cannot, and when would it be mistaken for having no answer?
A book against religion deserves a fair-minded reply. Proverbs on how to begin one: he that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him.
A hostile book is compared to those “written against Christ … by the Pharisees and Roman scholars.” Jesus: blessed are ye, when men shall say all manner of evil against you falsely, for my sake.
A hope for writers “proving the Cause of God with utmost eloquence.” Paul: I am set for the defence of the gospel.
A first answer, a second criticism, and then a full reply that surprised the critic. Proverbs: iron sharpeneth iron.
Read, memorize and reflect, so as to be ready with an answer. The Bereans: they searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
A prayer for a scholar “to prove Your religion, proclaim Your proof.” The psalmist: I will speak of thy testimonies also before kings, and will not be ashamed.
An “articulate response” had to be made. The Qur’án: Truth hath come and falsehood hath vanished away. Lo! falsehood is ever bound to vanish.
A history had been “poisoned and distorted.” Exodus: thou shalt not raise a false report.
A book half fabrication, with words altered. The Qur’án: confound not truth with falsehood, nor knowingly conceal the truth.
Some think “tales and legends” can discredit the Cause. Hamlet: be thou as chaste as ice, as pure as snow, thou shalt not escape calumny.

A report that a visitor returned from ‘Akká relieved to be rid of the Faith. Nehemiah’s reply to an open letter of rumours: there are no such things done as thou sayest, but thou feignest them out of thine own heart.
The Qur’án on what hearers of a slander owe: when ye heard it, said ye not: It is not for us to speak of this. This is awful calumny.
An editor meant to defame and printed, in the same paper, a letter that does the Cause credit. Joseph: ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good.

A response is to be shown to the fair-minded, and no copies given. Mill wanted every opinion to have its hearing: all silencing of discussion is an assumption of infallibility. What reasons might a persecuted community have for controlling where its own words go?

When a hostile sect does wrong, “they accuse the Bahá’ís, and the ill-wishers cry out that all are corrupt. But the truth will not remain hidden.” The householder of the parable is as patient: let both grow together until the harvest.
Large public gatherings would provoke the hostile; small ones are allowed. Jesus: I send you forth as sheep in the midst of wolves: be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves.
“Great caution is necessary.” Jesus: neither cast ye your pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet, and turn again and rend you.

“None should acknowledge that which he possesseth … Conceal the pearls of divine knowledge.” Jesus also said: neither do men light a candle, and put it under a bushel. When is concealment prudence and when is it a failure to shine? What in the reading’s circumstances decides it?
No one from the East is to be received without a signed letter. The early churches used the same safeguard, and Paul refers to it: need we, as some others, epistles of commendation to you?
“For wolves will come.” Paul to the elders of Ephesus: after my departing shall grievous wolves enter in among you, not sparing the flock.
Believers must not associate with one who comes without credentials. John: if there come any unto you, and bring not this doctrine, receive him not into your house.
Another New Testament letter says: be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares. How does a community stay hospitable and still protect itself?
Even one from ‘Akká itself is to be tested. John: believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God.
Men are sent “to mingle with you in order to throw suspicion upon those who are weak.” Jesus: beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep’s clothing.
Should one stand aside while a man with an axe undermines the foundation? Nehemiah’s builders: every one with one of his hands wrought in the work, and with the other hand held a weapon.
It is as well that such persons leave. John: they went out from us, but they were not of us.
With one “occupied with raising doubts … vigilance and protection” are necessary. Paul: mark them which cause divisions and offences, and avoid them.

Jefferson took the opposite risk with a nation: let them stand undisturbed as monuments of the safety with which error of opinion may be tolerated where reason is left free to combat it. What is different about a young religious community, on the readings’ account? What might it learn from Jefferson all the same?
Go in person, “with the utmost kindness and affection,” and answer the doubts. Paul: restore such an one in the spirit of meekness.
Each member must resist false rumours “like unto a great barrier.” Paul: that ye may be able to withstand in the evil day, and having done all, to stand.
Dispel doubts “through the power of proof.” Paul: in meekness instructing those that oppose themselves; if God peradventure will give them repentance to the acknowledging of the truth.
“Unsheath from the scabbard of thy mouth a tongue like unto the sword.” Paul: the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.

Arrive “like a piercing flame and striking lightning” and drive the doubter away. When two disciples wanted to call down fire on a village that refused them, Jesus rebuked them: ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of. How do the opening readings, on courtesy, govern the spirit of this one?
The Hands must “demolish these calumnies,” else malice whispers to every heedless soul. Proverbs: a whisperer separateth chief friends.
Protectors “like bars of iron” around “the mighty fortress of the Cause.” Proverbs: the name of the Lord is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe.
“A mighty fortress to defend His Faith.” Psalm 46, from which Luther took his hymn: God is our refuge and strength.
If the guardians of a house sleep, thieves enter. Jesus used the same picture: if the goodman of the house had known in what watch the thief would come, he would have watched.
“Great care and caution are needed.” The psalm adds what care depends on: except the Lord keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain.
Without protection “the very foundation” would be destroyed. Isaiah on guardians who failed: his watchmen are blind; they are all dumb dogs, they cannot bark; sleeping, lying down, loving to slumber.
“Ye are God’s hosts upon earth. Guard ye the fortress.” Paul: stand therefore, having your loins girt about with truth, and having on the breastplate of righteousness.
Safeguard the Cause “to the extent of your power.” Peter: be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary walketh about, seeking whom he may devour.

“The Divine sheep must constantly be guarded against devouring wolves.” Jesus: he that is an hireling seeth the wolf coming, and leaveth the sheep, and fleeth. The good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep.
“Guard thou the pearls of the love of God.” Paul: O Timothy, keep that which is committed to thy trust.
Guard the trust “through the hosts of steadfastness and righteousness.” Paul: the weapons of our warfare are not carnal.
“Protect ye the weak lest they follow every remote clamourer.” Paul: we then that are strong ought to bear the infirmities of the weak.
“The enemies of the Faith have been and are lying in wait.” Jesus: what I say unto you I say unto all, Watch.
“When His Cause is protected, we all remain protected.” Paul: whether one member suffer, all the members suffer with it.
“From every direction danger hath encircled the blessed Cause.” Paul: we are troubled on every side, yet not distressed; persecuted, but not forsaken.

Not to protect would be “connivance with the enemy.” Ezekiel on what a faithful shepherd does: I will seek that which was lost, and bring again that which was driven away, and will bind up that which was broken.
A speaker was hooted for quoting Bahá’u’lláh on love of mankind. Athens, hearing Paul: some mocked: and others said, We will hear thee again of this matter.
A critic judged a Prophet by a detail of his life. The reading names the essential proof; Jesus gave the rule: by their fruits ye shall know them.
Whoever wants the history of the Cause “must come to us and not go to those who are predisposed.” Philip to a sceptic: come and see.

Bacon’s advice to a reader: read not to contradict and confute; nor to believe and take for granted; but to weigh and consider. Would a fair inquirer hear only one side? What do the readings ask of the hostile sources, and of the inquirer?
Believers deal with accusations “convincingly.” Paul: let your speech be always with grace, seasoned with salt, that ye may know how ye ought to answer every man.
It is enough that they praise the Cause and deny false rumours. The Qur’án on those who will not join in idle talk: when they pass near senseless play, pass by with dignity.
Protectors who “shall not fear for their lives.” Paul: neither count I my life dear unto myself, so that I might finish my course with joy.
Pharaoh tried to extinguish the fire of the sacred Tree “with the waters of falsehood.” The Qur’án: fain would they put out the light of Allah with their mouths, but Allah will perfect His light.
The reading explains Isaiah 54:16. The verse: behold, I have created the smith that bloweth the coals in the fire; and I have created the waster to destroy.
And the verse that follows it: no weapon that is formed against thee shall prosper; and every tongue that shall rise against thee in judgment thou shalt condemn.
“My body hath borne imprisonment that your souls may be released.” Peter on the example that defence must not contradict: when he was reviled, reviled not again; when he suffered, he threatened not.
“No force of hosts can weaken Him.” Gamaliel: if it be of God, ye cannot overthrow it.
“I am he who fears no one.” The word to Jeremiah: be not afraid of their faces: for I am with thee to deliver thee.
Before princes and divines, “with the pen of justice and utterance.” Jesus, told to silence his followers: if these should hold their peace, the stones would immediately cry out.
A prayer to preserve “the fortress of Thy Cause.” Jesus: upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.

Protect it “from the perversion of the extremists.” Marcus Aurelius on a danger defenders run: the best way of avenging thyself is not to become like the wrong doer. How could the defence of a faith come to resemble what it resists?
“Strengthen his back and gird up his loins … and loose his tongue.” Isaiah: fear thou not; for I am with thee: I will strengthen thee; yea, I will help thee.
A prayer that the friends be “protected and preserved under the shadow of His grace.” The psalm: my help cometh from the Lord, which made heaven and earth.

The Revelation stands on “an unassailable, an enduring foundation.” Jesus: whosoever heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them, I will liken him unto a wise man, which built his house upon a rock.
There is an answer for everything, but believers often lack the scholarship to give it. Proverbs: the heart of the prudent getteth knowledge; and the ear of the wise seeketh knowledge.

nehemiah-one-hand-wrought-other-held-a-w.text: They which builded on the wall, and they that bare burdens, with those that laded, every one with one of his hands wrought in the work, and with the other hand held a weapon. For the builders, every one had his sword girded by his side, and so builded

isaiah-i-have-created-the-smith.text: Behold, I have created the smith that bloweth the coals in the fire, and that bringeth forth an instrument for his work; and I have created the waster to destroy

john-doth-our-law-judge-any-man.text: Doth our law judge any man, before it hear him, and know what he doeth

matthew-answered-him-to-never-a-word.text: And when he was accused of the chief priests and elders, he answered nothing. Then said Pilate unto him, Hearest thou not how many things they witness against thee? And he answered him to never a word; insomuch that the governor marvelled greatly

titus-convince-the-gainsayers.text: Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers

acts-mightily-convinced.text: For he mightily convinced the Jews, and that publicly, shewing by the scriptures that Jesus was Christ

deuteronomy-enquire-and-make-search.text: Then shalt thou enquire, and make search, and ask diligently; and, behold, if it be truth, and the thing certain, that such abomination is wrought among you
